blocks.text:
Design a Restaurant Management System that seats walk-in parties at the best-fitting table (the smallest available table whose capacity still fits the party, so a party of two is never seated at an empty table for eight), takes food orders against a menu, and tracks orders through a single kitchen that processes them one at a time, giving each order an estimated ready time based on how many orders are already queued ahead of it. Closing a table computes a bill from the items ordered plus tax.

  • Actors: Dining Party (requests a table, places an order), RestaurantService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: a single restaurant floor with tables of varying capacity, a shared menu, one serial kitchen queue, and per-table billing.

The distinguishing mechanic is best-fit resource assignment by size (a bin-packing-style pick, not first-available or lowest-id) combined with a kitchen queue whose estimated ready time depends on the prep time of every order already ahead of it, not a fixed duration.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Table inventory: define tables, each with a fixed seating capacity.
Seating: a party requests a table for N guests; the system assigns the smallest available table that still fits N.
Ordering: a seated party places an order made of one or more menu items.
Kitchen queue: orders are prepared one at a time, in the order they were placed; each order is given an estimated ready time.
Billing: closing a table computes a bill from all items ordered at that table plus tax, and frees the table.
Rejection: if no available table fits the party size, the request is rejected with a clear reason.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many tables, orders, and menu items must not require touching existing assignment logic.
Extensibility: a different assignment policy (e.g., preferring window tables) or a multi-station kitchen should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: table assignment, notification, and table creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: best-fit table assignment is O(tables), which stays small for a single restaurant floor.
Thread safety: two parties requesting the last table that fits their size concurrently must not both succeed.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Should a party ever be seated at a table larger than the best fit if no smaller one is free, or should that be a hard rejection?
Is the kitchen a single serial queue, or should different stations (grill, salad, dessert) prepare items in parallel?
Should estimated ready time be recalculated live as orders complete, or is a one-time estimate at placement time acceptable?
Should splitting a bill among party members be supported, or is a single total per table sufficient?
Are reservations (booked ahead of time) in scope, or is this walk-in seating only?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: Seating is walk-in only; advance reservations are out of scope for this design.

The kitchen is modeled as a single serial queue: orders are prepared strictly one after another, and within one order, items are assumed to cook in parallel so the order's own prep time is the maximum of its items' prep times, not their sum.
Estimated ready time is computed once, at placement time, and is not live-updated as earlier orders actually complete; this is a reasonable estimate rather than a real-time guarantee.
Bill splitting among party members is out of scope; each table receives a single combined bill.
Tax is a flat 8 percent of the subtotal; no tip calculation is modeled.

blocks.text: The design centers on five core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Table, MenuItem, Order, Kitchen Queue, Bill

items: Table: a seating unit with a fixed capacity and a status (AVAILABLE, OCCUPIED).
MenuItem: a purchasable dish with a price and a preparation time.
Order: a set of menu items placed by a table, with an estimated ready time.
Kitchen Queue: the FIFO sequence of orders not yet ready.
Bill: the computed subtotal, tax, and total for a table's order(s).

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A table hosts orders over time; an order references many menu items and produces one bill; the kitchen queue is a FIFO of orders

items: Table to Order is one-to-many over the table's lifetime.
Order to MenuItem is many-to-many (an order has several items; an item can appear on many orders).
Order to Bill is one-to-one, computed at table close.
Kitchen Queue holds a FIFO reference to active orders.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep table assignment, notification, and table creation decoupled from the core service.

Why needed: how a table is chosen for a given party size is a policy decision (best-fit today, perhaps "prefer window seating" or "prefer round tables for large parties" tomorrow) that changes independently of the seating workflow.

Why it is the best fit: a new assignment policy is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to RestaurantService. What it solves: it isolates a frequently-revised seating policy from stable orchestration logic.
Why needed: seating, rejections, order placement, and billing are all events a real restaurant system would want to react to (a host-stand display, a kitchen ticket printer, a receipt system).

metadata.alt: RestaurantObserver interface notified by RestaurantService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: RestaurantService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core seating and ordering workflow from side effects.
Why needed: table id generation should not be scattered across floor-plan setup code.
Why it is the best fit: configuring the floor plan becomes a handful of factory calls. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Table: attributes tableId, capacity, status; responsibility: track whether one seating unit is free.
TableFactory: method createTables(capacity, count); responsibility: generate capacity-prefixed table ids.
MenuItem: attributes name, price, prepTimeMinutes; responsibility: describe one purchasable dish.
Order: attributes orderId, tableId, items, estimatedReadyMinutes, status; responsibility: capture one order end-to-end.
RestaurantService: the orchestrator; responsibility: assign tables, place orders through the kitchen queue, compute bills, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: TableAssignmentStrategy and RestaurantObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: TableAssignmentStrategy: assignTable(partySize, availableTables): returns the chosen table, or null if none fit.
RestaurantObserver: onTableAssigned / onAssignmentRejected / onOrderPlaced / onBillGenerated: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: The end-to-end happy path, alongside its rejection branch, looks like this:

metadata.alt: Assign best-fit table, place order, compute estimated ready time from the queue, close table and bill

items: Seating path: request table → smallest fitting table free → assign, mark OCCUPIED.
Rejection path: request table → no available table fits the party size → rejected.
Ordering path: place order → compute own prep time (max of items) → add to the prep time of all orders already queued → estimated ready time returned.
Closing path: close table → sum item prices plus tax → bill returned, table freed.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: assignTable(partySize): finds and reserves the smallest fitting available table, or throws if none fit.
placeOrder(tableId, items): queues the order behind any already-queued orders and returns it with an estimated ready time.
markOrderReady(orderId): removes the order from the kitchen queue once its items are done.
closeTable(tableId): computes the bill for all orders at that table and frees the table.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: NoTableAvailableException: no available table has capacity for the requested party size.
InvalidOrderException: an order with an empty item list, or a reference to an unknown table.
TableNotOccupiedException: closeTable is called on a table that is not currently OCCUPIED.

blocks.text: The critical race is two parties requesting a table at the same moment when only one fitting table remains free.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing for the last fitting table; synchronization ensures only one is seated and the other is rejected or seated at a larger table

blocks.text: Synchronizing the best-fit-search-and-assign step across the whole table map ensures the check and the status update happen atomically, so only one party can ever claim a given table.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new assignment policy (prefer round tables, prefer a specific section) is a new TableAssignmentStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (kitchen display screen, host-stand pager) is a new RestaurantObserver implementation.
Multiple kitchen stations preparing different item categories in parallel can replace the single serial queue without changing the public API.
Reservations can be layered on top by pre-marking a table OCCUPIED-FOR-RESERVATION ahead of a scheduled time.
Single Responsibility: Table tracks seating state, TableAssignmentStrategy decides seating policy, RestaurantObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new assignment or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to RestaurantService.
Liskov Substitution: any TableAssignmentStrategy or RestaurantObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: RestaurantObserver exposes only the four lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: RestaurantService depends on the TableAssignmentStrategy and RestaurantObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
A party size exactly equal to a table's capacity is a valid fit (capacity is treated as inclusive, not strict).
Multiple tables share the exact same qualifying capacity: the lowest table id among them is chosen for a deterministic result.
An order with an empty item list is rejected with InvalidOrderException rather than silently queued with zero prep time.
Closing a table with no orders yet still produces a bill of zero.
assignTable: O(tables) to scan for the best-fit available table.
placeOrder: O(items in the order) for its own prep time, plus O(queue length) to sum preceding orders' prep times.
Space: O(tables + orders + queue length) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Table, Order, MenuItem, OrderItem, Bill

items: An index on Table(status, capacity) speeds up the "find the smallest fitting available table" query.
A junction table OrderItem records the many-to-many relationship between orders and menu items, with a quantity per line.
Recompute estimated ready times live as orders actually complete, instead of a one-time estimate at placement.
Support multiple parallel kitchen stations for different item categories.
Add bill splitting among party members.
In a distributed deployment, move table-status locking to a database-level row lock or a distributed lock rather than in-process synchronization.

# Observer interface: reacts to restaurant lifecycle events.
class RestaurantObserver:
    def on_table_assigned(self, table, party_size): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_assignment_rejected(self, party_size, reason): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_order_placed(self, order): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_bill_generated(self, table_id, bill): raise NotImplementedError

# Simple observer that prints events to the console.
class ConsoleRestaurantObserver(RestaurantObserver):
    def on_table_assigned(self, table, party_size):
        print(f"Table {table.table_id} assigned for party of {party_size}")

    def on_assignment_rejected(self, party_size, reason):
        print(f"Assignment rejected for party of {party_size}: {reason}")

    def on_order_placed(self, order):
        print(f"Order {order.order_id} placed for {order.table_id}, estimated ready in {order.estimated_ready_minutes} minutes")

    def on_bill_generated(self, table_id, bill):
        print(f"Bill for {table_id}: subtotal {bill.subtotal}, tax {bill.tax}, total {bill.get_total()}")

# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class NoTableAvailableException(Exception): pass
class InvalidOrderException(Exception): pass
class TableNotOccupiedException(Exception): pass

# The core orchestrator tying every piece together.
class RestaurantService:
    def __init__(self, assignment_strategy):
        self.tables = {}          # tableId -> Table
        self.orders = {}          # orderId -> Order
        self.table_orders = {}    # tableId -> all its orders, for billing
        self.kitchen_queue = []    # FIFO of orders not yet ready
        self.assignment_strategy = assignment_strategy  # pluggable seating policy
        self.observers = []         # listeners
        self.order_counter = 0      # simple id generator

    def add_table(self, table):
        self.tables[table.table_id] = table  # register a table
        self.table_orders[table.table_id] = []  # init its order list

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def assign_table(self, party_size):
        available = [t for t in self.tables.values() if t.is_available()]  # currently free tables
        chosen = self.assignment_strategy.assign_table(party_size, available)  # ask the strategy
        if chosen is None:  # nothing fits
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_assignment_rejected(party_size, "No table available")  # notify
            raise NoTableAvailableException(f"No table available for party size {party_size}")
        chosen.status = TableStatus.OCCUPIED  # claim the table
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_table_assigned(chosen, party_size)  # notify
        return chosen  # hand back to caller

    def place_order(self, table_id, items):
        if not items:
            raise InvalidOrderException("Order must contain at least one item")
        if table_id not in self.tables:
            raise InvalidOrderException(f"Unknown table: {table_id}")
        self.order_counter += 1                     # bump id counter
        order_id = f"ORD-{self.order_counter}"        # build id
        order = Order(order_id, table_id, items)       # build order
        ahead_minutes = sum(q.own_prep_time_minutes() for q in self.kitchen_queue)  # sum preceding orders
        order.estimated_ready_minutes = ahead_minutes + order.own_prep_time_minutes()  # this order waits behind all of them
        self.kitchen_queue.append(order)                # enqueue FIFO
        self.orders[order_id] = order                    # store it
        self.table_orders[table_id].append(order)          # track for billing
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_order_placed(order)  # notify
        return order  # hand back to caller

    def mark_order_ready(self, order_id):
        order = self.orders[order_id]  # look up order
        order.status = "READY"           # mark ready
        self.kitchen_queue.remove(order)  # leave the queue

    def close_table(self, table_id):
        table = self.tables.get(table_id)  # look up table
        if table is None or table.status != TableStatus.OCCUPIED:
            raise TableNotOccupiedException(f"Table {table_id} is not currently occupied")
        subtotal = sum(order.subtotal() for order in self.table_orders[table_id])  # sum all orders at this table
        tax = subtotal * 0.08  # flat 8 percent tax
        bill = Bill(subtotal, tax)  # build bill
        table.status = TableStatus.AVAILABLE  # free the table
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_bill_generated(table_id, bill)  # notify
        return bill  # hand back to caller

items: Why best-fit rather than first-available? First-available could seat a party of two at an empty eight-top, blocking it from a future large party; best-fit preserves large tables for large parties.

Why is an order's own prep time the maximum of its items rather than the sum? Because a real kitchen typically works on the items of one order in parallel (different stations), so the order is only as slow as its slowest item.

How would you support multiple kitchen stations instead of one serial queue? Partition MenuItem by a station field and maintain one FIFO queue per station, with an order's estimated ready time becoming the maximum across the stations its items touch.

Best-fit vs first-available table assignment: best-fit uses floor space more efficiently at the cost of a full O(tables) scan instead of stopping at the first match; for a restaurant-sized table count this is a clearly worthwhile trade.

Single serial kitchen queue vs per-station queues: a single queue is simple to reason about and implement, at the cost of not reflecting how most real kitchens actually parallelize work across stations.
One-time ready-time estimate vs live recalculation: a one-time estimate is cheap to compute and simple to test, at the cost of becoming stale if an earlier order runs long.
Persist tables, orders, and menu items in a relational database rather than in-memory maps, using the schema in the Database Design section.
Emit seating/order/billing events to a message queue so downstream systems (kitchen display, receipt printer, analytics) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Add idempotency keys to placeOrder so retried network requests cannot create duplicate orders.
Expose metrics on average kitchen queue wait time to help staffing decisions during peak hours.
